Author: Chief Justice Bench: Chief Justice  HIGH COURT OF JUDICATURE FOR RAJASTHAN  BENCH AT JAIPUR  S.B. Criminal Appeal No. 259/1990 Partap Singh son of Sardar Singh Rawat, resident of Kabra,
District Ajmer.
 ----Appellant  Versus State of Rajasthan  ----Respondent For Appellant(s) : Mr. Saurabh Bhagwati, Amicus Curiae For Respondent(s) : Mr. B.N. Sandu, Public Prosecutor

entities.text: HIGH COURT OF JUDICATURE FOR RAJASTHAN  BENCH AT JAIPUR
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text: HON'BLE THE CHIEF JUSTICE Judgment 19/02/2018 1.
Heard learned counsel for the parties.

2. The appellant has been convicted for offence punishable under Section 3/7 of the Essential Commodities Act and has been sentenced to undergo R.I. for a period of one year and pay fine in sum of `1,000/-.
In default of payment of fine he has been directed to undergo R.I. for three months.

3. As per the prosecution the appellant was employed as a salesman by the Kabra Sahkari Samiti and his duties were: (1) to receive rations to be distributed through the Public Distribution System,
(2) keep an account of the rations, (3) upon sale to the beneficiaries, maintain a record thereof.
60 bags of sugar and 40 tins of rapeseed oil were found missing.
They were recovered from the house of the appellant pursuant to a disclosure statement made by him.
4. At the trial the prosecution successfully proved Exhibit P-47 the order by which the appellant was appointed as a salesman in the Kabra Sahkari Samiti.
Exhibit P-55 is the order listing the duties of the appellant.
A perusal of Exhibit P-55 shows that the duties of the appellant are as were laid in the charge.

Exhibit P-7 is a report by one Devnarayan Vyas (PW30) as per which fictitious entries were Partap Singh vs State on 19 February, 2018 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/75094766/
1 made in the sales register showing distribution of sugar and rape seed oil to the registered consumers, but the fact being that the sales were not made.
5.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: A few registered consumers have been examined as PW-12, PW-13, PW-14 and PW-15 to PW-29 who have deposed that neither sugar nor rape seed oil was received by them.
Ration Cards Exhibit P-12 to Exhibit P-59 show that no entries regarding sale of sugar and rape seed oil is recorded therein.
6. It needs to be highlighted that pursuant to the disclosure statement made by the appellant, 60 bags of sugar and 34 tins of rapeseed oil were recovered from his house.
The bags had distinct marks of the Public Distribution System i.e. the department which had supplied the rations.
7. The documentary evidence establishes the charge and the recovery of 60 bags of sugar and 34 tins of rape seed oil seal the fate of the appellant.
The order Exhibit P-55 shows that the appellant was responsible for the distribution of the rations 8.
I find no infirmity in the impugned decision.
9. The incident relates to the year 1984.
10. Learned counsel for the appellant urges that the sentence may be reduced to the period already undergone which I find is too less.
During trial the appellant remained in custody only for two days and post conviction for three days.
Besides, minimum sentence prescribed by law is R.I. for a period of six months.
11. Learned counsel for the petitioner prays for directions to be issued as was done by the Supreme Court in the case reported as 1997 (9) SCC 101:N.Sukumaran Nair V/s Food Inspector.

In N.Sukumaran Nair's case (supra), the Supreme Court observed and directed as under:-
"The offence took place in the year 1984.

The appellant has been awarded six months'
simple imprisonment and has also been ordered to pay a fine of Rs.1000.
Under clause (d) of Section 433 of the Code of Criminal procedure, 'the appropriate government' is empowered to commute the sentence of simple imprisonment for fine.
We think that this would be an appropriate case for commutation of sentence where almost a decade has gone by.

We, therefore, direct the appellant to deposit in the trial court a sum of Rs.6000 as fine in commutation of the sentence of six months' (4 of 5) [CRLA-259/1990] simple imprisonment within a period of six weeks from today and intimate to the appropriate Government that such fine has been deposited.
On deposit of such fine, the State Government may formalise the matter by passing appropriate orders under clause (d) of Section 433 of the Code of Criminal Procedure."

14. I find that in a later judgment reported as 2004(5) SCC 721:Dayal Singh V/s State of Rajasthan,
the Supreme Court had observed as under:-
"15.

entities.text: 2004(5) SCC 721:Dayal Singh V/s State of Rajasthan
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In the instant case it was not disputed that for the offence charged a minimum sentence of 6 months' rigorous imprisonment is prescribed by law.
The appellant has been sentenced to undergo 6 months' rigorous imprisonment which is the minimum sentence.

We are not inclined to modify the sentence by passing an order of the nature passed in N. Sukumaran Nair where this Court in exercise of its extraordinary jurisdiction imposed only a sentence of fine and directed the State to exercise its powers under section 433 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to commute the sentence of simple imprisonment for fine.
In the instant case, the appellant has been sentenced to undergo 6 months' rigorous imprisonment.

Moreover, we are firmly of the view that strict adherence to the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act and the Rules framed thereunder is essential for safeguarding the interest of consumers of articles of food.
Stringent laws will have no meaning if offenders could get away with mere fine.
We, therefore, find no reason to interfere with the sentence imposed against the appellant."

15. Noting the two earlier decisions, in the decision reported as 2009(12) SCC 646:State of Rajasthan V/s Jagdish Prasad, the Supreme Court directed as under:-
"However, since the occurrence took place nearly three decades back if the accused respondent moves the appropriate Government to commute the sentence of imprisonment, the same shall be considered in the proper perspective.

entities.text: 2009(12) SCC 646:State of Rajasthan V/s Jagdish Prasad
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: For a period of three months, the accused need not surrender to undergo sentence during which period it shall be open to him to move the appropriate Government for commutation.

If no order in the matter of commutation is passed by the appropriate (5 of 5)
[CRLA-259/1990] Government the accused shall surrender to custody to serve the remainder of sentence."
Partap Singh vs State on 19 February, 2018 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/75094766/
3 16.

entities.text: Partap Singh vs State on 19 February, 2018 Indian Kanoon
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Since I am not inclined to interfere with the judgment of conviction and sentence passed, I would be inclined to issue the direction as was issued by the Supreme Court in Jagdish Prasad's case (supra).

17. Dismissing the appeal I suspend the sentence imposed upon the appellant for a period of six months directing that if the appellant makes a representation to the appropriate Government for commutation of sentence of imprisonment within one month, the same shall be considered by the appropriate Government and decision would be taken within four months thereafter.
The appellant need not surrender for a period of six months.
If the appropriate Government commutes the sentence, the appellant need not surrender.
If the petition seeking commutation is dismissed the appellant would suffer the remaining sentence.
(PRADEEP NANDRAJOG)C.J. KKC/JKP/s-1
